newsitem.title: USA: Holiday season's great time to look for job.
newsitem.headline: Holiday season's great time to look for job.

text.p: Job-seekers who believe the holiday season is not a good time to look for work could be left out in the cold.

Approached discreetly, the holiday party season is "a great time to look for a job," said Joelyn Cecere, senior vice president at outplacement firm Drake Beam Morin (DBM), New York. "In Manhattan, December is one of our highest placement months."

Many job candidates, Cecere said, tell her, "I'm not going to search that hard during the holiday time," when, she points out, Christmas parties offer them "a chance to network, meet new contacts and learn the inside scoop on companies in an informal social setting."
Cecere's firm specialises in helping employers find jobs for employees being terminated. Last year, DBM's global network of 166 offices served 4,000 companies relocating 270,000 people.

"Ten years ago people were ashamed of having lost a job," Cecere said. "But that has changed today. Downsizing is such a fixture of the corporate scene that almost everyone has had some experience with it. Because of this, many more people are willing to get out and network aggressively."

Besides, human resources executives "like to get hiring done before the first of the year," Cecere observes. "If your budget's been approved and you have those job spaces vacant and don't fill them, they take them back."
"It's also a pleasant thing to do some recruiting during the holidays as there's not the other business demands on an organisation and there's just a little more leeway in terms of time," she added.
Job-seekers should call ahead to friends and neighbours who are throwing Christmas parties as well as to sponsors of alumni group and charity parties to get themselves invited, Cecere said.

It's okay to arrive early and stay late in order to meet as many people as possible, "as long as you don't drink the whole time and get soused," Cecere said. "Find out ahead of time who is going to be at the party to help you target specific people you want to touch base with."
When the inevitable question "What do you do?" is asked, you could respond, "Like a lot of other people, I'm in transition right now," she advised.
"People are more open to networking during the holidays," she continued, "so talk a little about your profession and your job search."
The outplacement authority offered these holiday party tips:
-- "More is better. Go to as many parties as you can book yourself into."
-- Don't spend too much time with one person "until you've gotten around the room."

-- "Remember that you are at a holiday party so no bitterness, anger, regret or accusations for your former employer." Such expressions "are death in any interview situation" and "will do you more harm than good."
-- "Try early in the conversation to draw out of other people what they do for a living" -- a "first step to evaluating whether they can be a useful member of your network."
-- Show an interest "in non-work subjects"---shared friends, sports, schools, etc., connections that can be an "excellent icebreaker when you call them (employers) at work."
-- Unless someone is questioning you, "keep the actual work inquiry short" and, before leaving, get a business card and ask if you can call during business hours.

-- Don't hand out resumes. "It's easy to reject a resume but more difficult to reject a person," Cecere said. "You're really just asking for advice and information and when you pull out a resume that smacks of wanting that person to help you find a job."
-- "Don't forget it's a party. Not everyone is there to do business. So relax, have fun, and play it casual. Desperate is not attractive."
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
